lessons.title: 9.1 Reversible Reactions and Dynamic Equilibrium
lessons.notes_html:
Equilibrium is a Latin word meaning balance of forces. It is the state when there seems no change in a system, e.g. a pencil kept on a finger at rest.

Two Types of Equilibrium

  • Static equilibrium: the different phases remain at rest, e.g. the fulcrum and the playground seesaw.
  • Dynamic equilibrium: the phases readily interconvert, e.g. in vapour pressure the rate of evaporation equals the rate of condensation, so net change is zero.

Water, nitrogen, carbon dioxide and ozone cycles exist in dynamic equilibrium.

Reversible Reactions

Most chemical reactions are reversible: products can be transformed back into reactants. General form: A + B <=> C + D. The double-headed half arrow shows change in both directions. Chemical equilibrium is where the rate of producing C and D equals the rate of reproducing A and B.

  • Ammonia: 3H2(g) + N2(g) <=> 2NH3(g). NH3 can again give H2 and N2; NH3 is an important constituent of urea fertilizer.
  • N2O4(l) <=> 2NO2(g) at 140C: N2O4 is pale yellow (liquid), NO2 is reddish brown (gas).
  • H2(g) + I2(g) <=> 2HI(g): colourless H2 + purple I2 form colourless HI, which decomposes back.
  • Sulphur trioxide: 2SO2(g) + O2(g) <=> 2SO3(g).

In the H2 + I2 graph, H2 and I2 concentrations fall and HI rises, then all become constant. At equilibrium all three species are present, the reaction does not stop, and rate of forward reaction = rate of reverse reaction. All reactions are reversible, but the extent of reversibility varies greatly.

Key Points

  • Equilibrium means balance of forces and no apparent change in the system.
  • Static equilibrium is at rest; dynamic equilibrium has equal opposite changes and zero net change.
  • A reversible reaction is written with <=>, e.g. 3H2 + N2 <=> 2NH3.
  • At dynamic equilibrium forward and reverse rates are equal and concentrations stay constant.
  • The reaction does not stop at equilibrium; all species remain present.

lessons.title: 9.2 Law of Mass Action and Derivation of the Expression for the Equilibrium Constant
lessons.notes_html:
In 1864 two scientists, Guldberg and Waage, studied the relation of dynamic equilibrium with quantities or concentration and put forward the law of mass action.

Law of Mass Action

The rate of a chemical reaction is directly proportional to the product of active masses (or concentration) of reactants at constant temperature.

Derivation for A + B <=> C + D

  • Forward reaction: A + B -> C + D
  • Reverse reaction: C + D -> A + B
  • Rate of forward reaction Rf = Kf [A] [B]
  • Rate of reverse reaction Rr = Kr [C] [D]

Here [ ] shows molar concentration and Kf, Kr are proportionality constants.

At dynamic equilibrium the rates are equal: Rf = Rr, so Kf [A] [B] = Kr [C] [D]. Rearranging: Kf / Kr = [C] [D] / ([A] [B]). As Kf and Kr are both constants, Kf / Kr = Kc, the equilibrium constant.

Therefore: Kc = [C] [D] / ([A] [B])

General Form and Kp

For aA + bB <=> cC + dD: Kc = [C]^c [D]^d / ([A]^a [B]^b), where a, b, c and d are the reaction coefficients, written as powers.

In gaseous systems, partial pressure of gases is taken instead of concentration, so Kp is used instead of Kc. For aA(g) + bB(g) <=> cC(g) + dD(g): Kp = (pC)^c (pD)^d / ((pA)^a (pB)^b), where p is the partial pressure of a gas.

Key Points

  • Law of mass action was given by Guldberg and Waage in 1864.
  • Rate is directly proportional to the product of active masses of reactants at constant temperature.
  • At equilibrium Rf = Rr, which gives Kc = [C] [D] / ([A] [B]).
  • In the general expression, each concentration is raised to the power of its coefficient.
  • For gases, Kp uses partial pressures instead of concentrations.

lessons.title: 9.3 Equilibrium Constant and Its Units
lessons.notes_html:
The equilibrium constant Kc tells us the concentration of different species of the reaction at both the reactant and product sides at the time of equilibrium.

Kc = Product of the concentration of products raised to the power of coefficient / Product of the concentration of reactants raised to the power of coefficient.

It helps in calculating the concentration of species of a reaction, and with suitable applications we can enhance the quantity of the desired species of a reversible reaction.

What Kc Depends On

  • Kc depends upon temperature: if temperature is changed, its value also changes.
  • Kc does not depend upon the initial concentration of reactants or products.

Units of Kc

Kc is a ratio, so units may cancel. Its units vary from case to case.

ReactionKc ExpressionUnits
H2(g) + I2(g) <=> 2HI(g) at 450CKc = [HI]^2 / ([H2] [I2])No units: (mol dm-3)^2 / ((mol dm-3)(mol dm-3)) cancel
N2(g) + 3H2(g) <=> 2NH3(g) at 450CKc = [NH3]^2 / ([N2] [H2]^3)(mol dm-3)^-2, because moles of reactants and products are not equal

So: when the number of moles of reactants and products are equal, Kc has no units; when they are not equal, Kc has units.

Key Points

  • Kc is the ratio of product concentrations to reactant concentrations, each raised to its coefficient.
  • Kc changes only with temperature, not with initial concentrations.
  • For H2 + I2 <=> 2HI, Kc has no units.
  • For N2 + 3H2 <=> 2NH3, Kc has units (mol dm-3)^-2.
  • Units of Kc vary from case to case.

lessons.title: 9.4 Importance of Equilibrium Constant
lessons.notes_html:
The equilibrium constant has many applications in chemistry. The value of Kc is used to calculate important phenomena of reversible reactions used in industries.

Industrial Use

Kc is used to calculate the amount of reactants or products of reversible reactions of industrially important compounds like sulphuric acid (H2SO4), nitric acid (HNO3), urea CO(NH2)2.

Increasing the Yield of Ammonia

For NH3, used in synthesis of urea fertilizer: N2(g) + 3H2(g) <=> 2NH3(g) at 450C, and Kp = (NH3)^2 / ((N2) (H2)^3). Kp has a constant value, so to increase NH3:

  • Increase the concentration / pressure of N2.
  • Increase the concentration / pressure of H2.
  • Decrease the amount of NH3 by removal.

Then more NH3 is formed and hence more urea can be formed.

Predicting Direction and Extent

  • Kc is used to predict the direction of a chemical reaction and, after a specific time, its extent.
  • Very high Kc: concentration of products is very high at equilibrium, so the desired product can be easily made.
  • Very low Kc: concentration of initial reactants is high at equilibrium, so the reaction is not feasible.
  • Kc helps calculate the effect of changing conditions, so the yield can be controlled; this decreases expenditure of preparation and product prices can be controlled to a desired level.

Key Points

  • Kc is used in industry for H2SO4, HNO3 and urea manufacture.
  • More NH3 is obtained by increasing N2 or H2 and by removing NH3.
  • High Kc means products dominate and the reaction is feasible.
  • Low Kc means reactants dominate and the reaction is not feasible.
  • Kc predicts direction and extent and helps control yield.

lessons.title: 10.1 Concepts of Acids and Bases
lessons.notes_html:
General Properties of Acids

The word acid comes from Latin acidus meaning sour. Acids taste sour: acetic acid in vinegar, citric acid in lemons, grapefruit, oranges and limes, and lactic acid in sour milk, yogurt and cottage cheese, formed by fermentation of lactose sugar. Citrus sourness is also due to ascorbic acid.

  • Acids turn blue litmus red. Litmus is the oldest known pH indicator: red in acid, blue in base.
  • Acids corrode active metals: acid + metal -> salt + hydrogen gas. Even gold is attacked by aqua regia, a mixture of acids.
  • Acid solutions conduct electricity because acids ionize in water and ions are present.

General Properties of Bases

Bases taste bitter, turn red litmus blue and have a slippery, soapy touch in dilute solution. Strong concentrated acids and bases are corrosive and must not be touched.

Arrhenius Concept

According to Arrhenius, an acid yields hydrogen / hydronium ions in water, e.g. HCl(aq) -> H+(aq) + Cl-(aq), and a base yields hydroxide ions, e.g. NaOH(aq) -> Na+(aq) + OH-(aq). This concept is limited to aqueous solutions and cannot explain the basic character of ammonia, NH3.

Key Points

  • Acids are sour, turn blue litmus red, corrode metals giving H2, and conduct electricity in water.
  • Bases are bitter and slippery, and turn red litmus blue.
  • Arrhenius: acid gives H+ in water; base gives OH- in water.
  • Arrhenius concept works only for aqueous solutions.

lessons.title: 10.1.2 The Bronsted-Lowry Concept
lessons.notes_html:
Bronsted-Lowry Definitions (1923)

In 1923 J.N. Bronsted and T.M. Lowry independently proposed a broader concept. A Bronsted-Lowry acid is any substance capable of donating a proton (H+) to another substance. A Bronsted-Lowry base is any substance capable of accepting a proton (H+). A proton is what is left when a hydrogen atom loses an electron to become an ion.

HCl(aq) + H2O(l) -> H3O+(aq) + Cl-(aq): HCl is the acid, H2O is the base as it accepts H+. H2SO4(aq) + H2O(l) -> H3O+(aq) + HSO4-(aq).

Conjugate Acids and Bases

When HCl transfers H+ to H2O, the H3O+ formed is the conjugate acid (formed from the parent base) and Cl- is the conjugate base (formed from the parent acid). Similarly HSO4- is a conjugate base.

Polyprotic Acids and Strength

Acids that can donate more than one proton are polyprotic acids, e.g. H2SO4 and H3PO4. Strength depends on tendency to donate / accept protons: HCl is a very strong acid, while citric acid in lemon is relatively weaker. This theory cannot explain the acidic character of SO2, NO2, AlCl3 and BF3, or the basic character of CaO and MgO.

Key Points

  • Bronsted-Lowry acid = proton (H+) donor; base = proton acceptor.
  • Conjugate acid forms from a base; conjugate base forms from an acid.
  • H2SO4 and H3PO4 are polyprotic acids.
  • Stronger acids donate protons more readily; stronger bases accept them more readily.

lessons.title: 10.1.3 The Lewis Concept
lessons.notes_html:
Lewis Definitions (1923)

In 1923 G. N. Lewis (1875-1946) gave a more general concept, based on electron pairs instead of only proton transfer. When H+ combines with OH- to form water, H+ accepts a pair of electrons from OH- to form a new covalent bond.

  • Lewis acid: any substance that can act as an electron-pair acceptor, e.g. the H+ ion. Anything with one or more empty valence-shell orbitals can act as a Lewis acid.
  • Lewis base: any substance that can act as an electron-pair donor, e.g. the OH- ion. Every Bronsted base must have a pair of nonbonding electrons to accept a proton.

Example: BF3 and NH3

BF3 reacts instantaneously with NH3. The nonbonding electrons on nitrogen in NH3 are donated into an empty orbital on boron in BF3, forming a new type of covalent bond called a coordinate covalent bond: BF3 + NH3 -> BF3-NH3.

The Lewis concept has a marked edge over previous theories: it explains not only hydrogen-containing acids but also species that lack H+, and explains bases in a comprehensive manner.

Key Points

  • Lewis acid = electron-pair acceptor; Lewis base = electron-pair donor.
  • H+ is a Lewis acid and OH- is a Lewis base.
  • NH3 donates its lone pair to BF3, forming a coordinate covalent bond.
  • Lewis theory is the broadest of the three concepts.

lessons.title: 10.2 The pH Scale (Hydrogen Ion Concentration)
lessons.notes_html:
Self-Ionization of Water and pH

Water molecules react with each other: H2O(l) + H2O(l) -> H3O+(aq) + OH-(aq). This is the self-ionization of water. Its dissociation constant is Kw = [H+][OH-] = 1 x 10^-14. In pure water [H+] = [OH-] = 1 x 10^-7.

pH = -log[H+]. For pure water, -log[H+] = 7, so pH 7 is neutral. pH 1 to 6.9 is acidic, pH 7.1 to 14.0 is basic. Lower pH means more acidic: pH 2 is more acidic than pH 3. Higher pH means more basic: pH 10 is more basic than pH 8.

Example 10.1: If [H+] = 0.0001 moles/lit = 1 x 10^-4, then pH = -log(1 x 10^-4) = 4.

Key Points

  • Kw = [H+][OH-] = 1 x 10^-14; pure water has pH 7.
  • pH = -log[H+]; pH below 7 is acidic, above 7 is basic.
  • As pH decreases, [H+] and acidic character increase.
  • Phenolphthalein is colourless in acid and pink in base; methyl orange is red in acid and yellow in base.

lessons.title: 10.3 The Salts
lessons.notes_html:
What is a Salt?

Salts are the neutralization products when an acid reacts with a base: HCl(aq) + NaOH(s) -> NaCl(aq) + H2O(l). Similarly H2SO4(aq) + 2KOH(aq) -> K2SO4(aq) + 2H2O(l). Salts are ionic compounds with high melting and boiling points, e.g. NaCl melts at 801 C. Thousands of salts exist and most inorganic compounds belong to this class.

Colour, Taste and Odour

Many salts are coloured: yellow sodium chromate, orange potassium dichromate, blue copper sulfate pentahydrate, colourless magnesium sulfate. Salts show all five tastes: salty NaCl, sour potassium bitartrate, bitter magnesium sulfate, and umami monosodium glutamate. Salts of strong acids and strong bases are non-volatile and odourless.

Key Points

  • A salt plus water is formed when an acid neutralizes a base.
  • Salts are ionic, with high melting and boiling points; NaCl melts at 801 C.
  • NaCl is used in food, (NH4)3PO4 as fertilizer and AgNO3 in photography.
  • Potassium dichromate is orange and copper sulphate is blue.

lessons.title: 10.3.1 Preparation of Salts
lessons.notes_html:
Natural Sources

Many salts are obtained by mining: CaCO3 (lime and marble), halite NaCl, gypsum CaSO4.2H2O and NaHCO3. In Pakistan the world's second largest halite mine is at Khewra, near Jhelum. NaCl is also got by evaporating sea water.

Preparation of Soluble Salts

  • Acid + base: HCl + NaOH -> NaCl + H2O.
  • Acid + metal: H2SO4 + 2Na -> Na2SO4 + H2; 2HCl + Ca -> CaCl2 + H2.
  • Acid + metallic oxide: 2HCl + CuO -> CuCl2 + H2O; H2SO4 + MgO -> MgSO4 + H2O.
  • Acid + metal carbonate: H2SO4 + Na2CO3 -> Na2SO4 + H2O + CO2.

Insoluble salts are made by precipitation: mix two soluble salt solutions and filter off the precipitate, e.g. CaCl2 + K2SO4 -> 2KCl + CaSO4(s).

10.3.2 Types of Salts

  • Normal / neutral: no H+ or OH- in water, e.g. NaCl, KCl, K2SO4.
  • Acidic: produce H+ or accept a lone pair, e.g. KHSO4, AlCl3, NH4Cl.
  • Basic: produce OH- or accept H+, e.g. Na2CO3.10H2O, NaHCO3, CH3COONa.
  • Double: made of two salts, e.g. Mohr's salt FeSO4.(NH4)2SO4.6H2O and potash alum.

10.3.3 Uses of Salts

Uses: in food (NaCl, monosodium glutamate, NaHCO3), as pigments (orange K2Cr2O7, green NiCl2, yellow CdS), as preservatives (Na2S2O5, NaCl), in medicines (Epsom salt MgSO4.7H2O as purgative, fluoride salts for tooth decay, calcium salts for bones), as fertilizers (KNO3, ammonium phosphate), in glass making (sodium silicate) and as bleaching powder Ca(OCl)Cl. Sea water has about 35,000 ppm salt; it is desalinated by reverse osmosis.

Key Points

  • Soluble salts are made by acid with base, metal, metal oxide or metal carbonate.
  • Insoluble salts are made by precipitation and separated by filtration.
  • Salts are normal, acidic, basic or double salts.
  • Khewra has the world's second largest halite mine.

lessons.title: 11.1 Introduction to Organic Chemistry
lessons.notes_html:
What is Organic Chemistry?

Organic chemistry is the branch of chemistry that deals with hydrocarbons and their derivatives. Hydrocarbons are compounds containing only carbon and hydrogen. Carbon is the chief element in organic compounds. Examples are methane CH4, glucose C6H12O6, urea and proteins.

Compounds containing carbon but studied as inorganic include oxides of carbon, carbonates, bicarbonates, cyanides and carbides, e.g. NaHCO3 is inorganic.

Vital Force Theory and Wohler

Berzelius in 1815 proposed the vital force theory: organic compounds could only be made by living organisms with a vital force. In 1828 Wohler broke this theory by preparing urea, the first synthetic organic compound, in the laboratory by heating ammonium cyanate: NH4CNO -> NH2CONH2 (urea). After this, many organic compounds were synthesised in laboratories.

Key Points

  • Organic chemistry studies hydrocarbons and their derivatives; carbon is the chief element.
  • Hydrocarbons contain only carbon and hydrogen, e.g. CH4.
  • Vital force theory (Berzelius, 1815) said organic compounds need a living source.
  • Wohler (1828) made urea from ammonium cyanate, ending vitalism.

lessons.title: 11.1 Features of Organic Compounds
lessons.notes_html:
General Characteristics

  • Mostly covalent compounds, generally non-polar.
  • Insoluble in water, soluble in organic solvents.
  • Low melting and boiling points; mostly liquids or low-melting solids, volatile and inflammable.
  • Reactions are slow and often need heat, pressure or a catalyst.
  • Show isomerism: same molecular formula, different structures, e.g. butane and isobutane, both C4H10.

Catenation and Homologous Series

Catenation is the ability of carbon to link with itself to form long straight chains, branched chains and rings. This is why millions of organic compounds exist.

A homologous series is a family with the same functional group and similar chemical properties, where each member differs by a -CH2- unit and physical properties change regularly. In alkanes boiling point rises with chain length: methane (1 C) -162 C, ethane (2 C) -89 C, propane (3 C) -42 C, butane (4 C) 0 C, pentane (5 C) 36 C, n-hexane (6 C) 69 C.

Key Points

  • Organic compounds are covalent, non-polar, water-insoluble and have low melting/boiling points.
  • Catenation = carbon forming long chains, branches and rings with itself.
  • Homologous series members differ by CH2, share chemical properties.
  • Isomers have the same formula but different structures.

lessons.title: 11.2 Sources of Organic Compounds
lessons.notes_html:
Main Sources

The main source is the plant kingdom (photosynthesis in green plants). Animals get organic compounds from plants. Buried decayed plants and animals, under heat and pressure, formed coal, petroleum and natural gas.

11.2.1 Coal

TypeCarbon %Use

11.2.2 Petroleum and 11.2.3 Natural Gas

Petroleum (Petra = rock, Oleum = oil) is a blackish viscous liquid, a mixture of hundreds of compounds. It is purified by fractional distillation on the basis of different boiling points: Refinery gases C1-C4 (cylinder gas), Gasoline C4-C8 (car fuel), Naphtha C5-C10 (making chemicals), Kerosene C12-C16 (aircraft fuel), Diesel C15-C18, Fuel oil C19-C30 (ships, power stations), Residue 400-600 C (bitumen for roads and roofs).

Natural gas, found at Sui, Balochistan in 1952, hence called Sui gas, contains: methane 70-90%, ethane 5-15%, propane less than 5%, butane 1-2%, rest N2, CO2, H2S. Used as fuel, CNG and for urea. In LPG, propane and butane proportion is higher to ease liquefaction.

11.2.4 Synthesis: many compounds are now made in laboratories/factories, e.g. plastics, urea, medicines, detergents, dyes, artificial fibres.

Key Points

  • Plants are the main source; coal, petroleum and natural gas formed from buried remains.
  • Anthracite >90% C is best coal; peat about 60% C is inferior.
  • Petroleum fractions are separated by fractional distillation by boiling point.
  • Natural gas is mainly methane 70-90%; Sui gas found in 1952.

lessons.title: 11.3 Uses of Organic Compounds
lessons.notes_html:
Organic Compounds in Daily Life

Because of catenation, organic compounds are countless and are used at almost every step of daily life:

  • Food: vegetables, fruits, meat and cereals are organic compounds.
  • Clothing: natural fibres cotton and wool, and artificial fibres like rayon and plastic threads.
  • Medicines: antipyretics, anti-inflammatory drugs, antihistamines, antibiotics and anti-ulcer drugs.
  • Fertilisers: urea and others increase crop production.
  • Insecticides and fungicides: used against insect and fungus attack.
  • Fuels: natural gas, petrol, kerosene oil, diesel, CNG, LPG, coal and wood.
  • Dyes: give colour in daily life.
  • Plastics: used in various fields of life.

Key Points

  • Food, clothes, medicines, fertilisers and fuels are mostly organic compounds.
  • Medicines such as antibiotics and antipyretics are organic.
  • Urea fertiliser, dyes, plastics and fibres are important uses.
  • Organic chemistry affects almost every part of our life.

lessons.title: 11.4 Alkanes and Alkyl Radicals
lessons.notes_html:
Alkanes

Alkanes are the simplest class, with carbon linked by single covalent bonds only. General formula CnH2n+2. They are saturated hydrocarbons because each carbon forms its maximum 4 bonds. First members: methane CH4, ethane C2H6, propane C3H8, butane C4H10, pentane C5H12, hexane C6H14, heptane C7H16, octane C8H18, nonane C9H20, decane C10H22. Condensed formula of hexane is CH3(CH2)4CH3. Compounds with same formula but different structures are isomers, e.g. butane/isobutane and pentane/isopentane/neopentane.

Alkanes are water-insoluble, less reactive, and burn to give much energy, so used as fuels: CH4 + 2O2 -> CO2 + 2H2O + 891 KJ/mol; C3H8 + 5O2 -> 3CO2 + 4H2O + 2220 KJ/mol. Alkanes with more than 20 carbons are lubricants; paraffin wax (20-40 carbons) is used in candles, lubricants, water repellents and skin creams.

11.4.1 Alkyl Radicals and Classification

Removing one H from an alkane gives an alkyl group, written R-H for the class, with an unpaired electron: methane -> methyl .CH3, ethane -> ethyl .C2H5; also n-propyl, isopropyl, n-butyl, isobutyl. Suffix -ane changes to -yl.

Alkanes are classified as straight chain (each C bonded to max 2 other C, e.g. n-pentane), branched (at least one C bonded to 3 other C) and cyclic (closed ring, at least 3 C, e.g. cyclopropane, cyclobutane, cyclohexane). Carbon atoms may be primary (linked to 1 C), secondary (2 C), tertiary (3 C) or quaternary (4 C).

Key Points

  • Alkanes: CnH2n+2, single bonds, saturated hydrocarbons.
  • Combustion gives CO2 + H2O + heat; higher alkanes give more energy.
  • Alkyl radical = alkane minus one H, e.g. methyl .CH3.
  • Alkanes are straight chain, branched or cyclic.

lessons.title: 11.5 The Functional Groups
lessons.notes_html:
What is a Functional Group?

A functional group is the group of atom(s) upon which the functions or properties of an organic compound depend. It is the most reactive part of the compound. Compounds with the same functional group form the same homologous series, with same chemical properties. Fruit fragrance is due to the ester group, e.g. banana has isopentyl acetate, apple methyl butyrate, orange octyl acetate.

  • Alcohols are R-OH, carboxylic acids R-COOH, ethers R-O-R'.

lessons.title: 12.1 Hydrocarbons
lessons.notes_html:
What are Hydrocarbons?

Hydrocarbons are compounds containing only carbon and hydrogen. They are the simplest organic compounds and the parent compounds of all other organic compounds. They occur in petroleum, natural gas and coal, formed from dead plants and animals buried under the earth millions of years ago. They are mostly used as fuels.

Classification

  • Open chain (aliphatic) compounds: carbon atoms form a chain, e.g. n-butane (straight chain) and 2-methylpropane (branched chain).
  • Closed chain (cyclic) compounds: carbons form a ring. Alicyclic, e.g. cyclobutane, have properties like aliphatic compounds. Aromatic, e.g. benzene, have a ring of alternate single and double bonds.
  • Saturated hydrocarbons have only single bonds, e.g. ethane. Unsaturated hydrocarbons have double or triple bonds, e.g. ethene and ethyne.

Carbon atoms are primary (joined to 1 carbon), secondary (2 carbons), tertiary (3 carbons) or quaternary (4 carbons).

Key Points

  • Hydrocarbons contain only C and H and come from petroleum, natural gas and coal.
  • Two main classes: open chain (aliphatic) and closed chain (cyclic).
  • Cyclic compounds are alicyclic or aromatic (e.g. benzene).
  • Single bonds = saturated; double/triple bonds = unsaturated.

lessons.title: 12.2 The Alkanes
lessons.notes_html:
The Alkanes

Alkanes have only single bonds between carbon atoms. Carbon forms 4 bonds, so alkanes cannot add more atoms and are saturated compounds. General formula: CnH2n+2. Names end with suffix ane. They are insoluble in water, dissolve in non-polar solvents, are relatively inert, and are used as fuel and lubricating oil.

Methane, CH4, is the first member. It has a regular tetrahedral structure: H-C-H angle 109.5 degrees, C-C length 1.54 A (154 pm) and C-H length 1.10 A (110 pm). Alkanes are obtained from natural gas and petroleum by fractional distillation. Cyclic alkanes do not follow CnH2n+2.

Naming Alkanes (12.2.1)

IUPAC naming uses a root name for the longest chain: 1 = Meth, 2 = Eth, 3 = Prop, 4 = But, 5 = Pent. Branches are named as radicals and numbered from the end giving the lowest number, e.g. 2-methylbutane and 2,2-dimethylpropane (common name neopentane).

Key Points

  • Alkanes: single bonds only, saturated, general formula CnH2n+2, suffix ane.
  • First ten members run methane to decane (C10H22).
  • Methane is tetrahedral with bond angle 109.5 degrees.
  • IUPAC name = branch position + branch name + longest-chain root + ane.

lessons.title: 12.2.2 Preparation of Alkanes
lessons.notes_html:
Preparation of Alkanes (12.2.2)

1. Hydrogenation: addition of hydrogen to alkenes and alkynes in presence of Ni, Pt or Pd catalyst gives alkanes. Ethene + H2 -> ethane (Ni, 250-300 C). Ethyne is hydrogenated in two steps: ethyne -> ethene -> ethane.

2. Reduction of alkyl halides: alkyl halides are reduced with Zn/HCl at room temperature, e.g. ethyl chloride + 2[H] -> ethane + HCl.

Physical Properties (12.2.3)

Alkanes are covalent, non-polar compounds. Melting and boiling points increase with carbon number. First four members are gases, from 5 carbons they are liquids, and above 20 carbons they are waxy solids. They dissolve in non-polar solvents like benzene.

Chemical Properties (12.2.4)

Alkanes are less reactive, so they are called paraffins. Halogenation: in light, Cl2 replaces H atoms step by step: CH4 + Cl2 -> CH3Cl + HCl, then CH2Cl2, CHCl3 and finally CCl4. Combustion: complete oxidation gives CO2 and water with much energy: CH4 + 2O2 -> CO2 + 2H2O, 890 KJ/mole; propane gives 2219 KJ/mole.

Key Points

  • Alkanes are prepared by hydrogenation (Ni/Pd) and by reduction of alkyl halides (Zn/HCl).
  • C1-C4 are gases, C5 onwards liquids, above C20 waxy solids.
  • Halogenation in light replaces H by Cl one by one up to CCl4.
  • Combustion of methane releases 890 KJ/mole.

lessons.title: 12.3 The Alkenes
lessons.notes_html:
The Alkenes

Alkenes are unsaturated hydrocarbons with at least one double bond. General formula: CnH2n (for one double bond). Suffix ane is replaced by ene. Examples: ethene H2C=CH2, propene CH2=CH-CH3, 1-butene and 2-butene. They are more reactive than alkanes and are used as starting material for many organic compounds. They are also called olefins (oil-forming).

Preparation (12.3.1)

  • Dehydration of alcohols: ethanol with conc. H2SO4 at 170 C gives ethene: CH3CH2OH -> CH2=CH2 + H2O.
  • Dehydrohalogenation: removing HX from alkyl halides with alcoholic KOH at 100 C, e.g. ethyl bromide -> ethene + KBr + H2O.

Reactions and Uses (12.3.2)

  • Addition of halogens: at room temperature in CCl4, e.g. propene + Cl2 -> dichloropropane.
  • Hydrohalogenation: CH2=CH2 + HBr -> ethyl bromide; used to prepare alkyl halides.
  • Oxidation: 1% alkaline KMnO4 (Baeyer's reagent) gives glycols and its pink colour is discharged - a test for a double bond.

Uses: making polythene, glycols, alcohols and halogen derivatives. Hydrogenation of alkenes makes ghee. Ethene is used for polythene plastic, ripening fruits and as a general anaesthetic.

Key Points

  • Alkenes: at least one double bond, general formula CnH2n, suffix ene.
  • Prepared by dehydration of alcohols and dehydrohalogenation of alkyl halides.
  • They give addition reactions; KMnO4 pink colour is discharged (Baeyer test).
  • Ethene is used for polythene and for ripening fruits.

lessons.title: 12.4 The Alkynes
lessons.notes_html:
The Alkynes

Alkynes are unsaturated hydrocarbons with at least one triple bond, so they are more unsaturated than alkenes. General formula: CnH2n-2, suffix yne. Examples: ethyne (acetylene) HC=CH in triple bond form C2H2, propyne and 1-butyne. Acetylene burns with oxygen at very high temperature: 2C2H2 + 5O2 -> 4CO2 + 2H2O + heat, so it is used in oxy-acetylene torches for cutting and welding metals.

Preparation (12.4.1)

  • Dehydrohalogenation of vicinal dihalides: halogens on adjacent carbons are removed with alcoholic KOH, e.g. vicinal dibromide + 2KOH -> ethyne + 2KBr + 2H2O.
  • Dehalogenation of tetrahalides: with Zn dust, e.g. 1,1,2,2-tetrabromoethane + 2Zn -> ethyne + 2ZnBr2.

Properties, Reactions and Uses

First members are gases; boiling and melting points rise with chain length and are higher than corresponding alkenes. They are non-polar, insoluble in water, and dissolve in benzene and ether. Alkynes are reactive but generally less reactive than alkenes. Addition of halogens: ethyne + 2Cl2 -> 1,1,2,2-tetrachloroethane at room temperature. Oxidation: KMnO4 in acid breaks the triple bond: ethyne + 4[O] -> oxalic acid; this locates the triple bond. Uses: starting material for PVC, synthetic rubber, alcohols and alkyl halides; acetylene is used for welding and artificial ripening of fruits like mangoes. Calcium carbide gives acetylene with water: CaC2 + 2H2O -> C2H2 + Ca(OH)2.

Key Points

  • Alkynes: at least one triple bond, general formula CnH2n-2, suffix yne.
  • Prepared from vicinal dihalides (alcoholic KOH) and tetrahalides (Zn dust).
  • Ethyne + Cl2 gives tetrachloroethane; KMnO4 oxidation gives oxalic acid.
  • Acetylene is used in oxy-acetylene welding and fruit ripening.

lessons.title: 13.1 Carbohydrates
lessons.notes_html:
Biochemistry studies compounds in living organisms: carbohydrates, proteins, lipids, nucleic acids and vitamins.

What are Carbohydrates?

Carbohydrates are the most abundant bio-compounds, used mostly as a source of energy. General formula Cx(H2O)y, so called hydrates of carbon. Glucose is C6H12O6; sucrose, C12H22O11, does not fit. They are polyhydroxy aldehydes or ketones: many -OH groups with -CHO (glucose) or a ketonic group (fructose). Made by photosynthesis: 6CO2 + 6H2O -> C6H12O6 + 6O2 (chlorophyll, sunlight).

Classification

  • Monosaccharides (1 unit): white, water-soluble, crystalline, sweet; building blocks of the others. First member glyceraldehyde, C3H6O3, has three carbons. Others: glucose, fructose (fruit sugar), galactose, ribose C5H10O5.
  • Oligosaccharides (2-10 units, loss of water): sucrose = glucose + fructose, lactose = glucose + galactose, maltose = glucose + glucose.
  • Polysaccharides (more than 10): starch, glycogen, cellulose - all glucose units, differing in sequence.

Sources and Uses

CarbohydrateSource
GlucoseGrapes
FructoseFruits, honey
SucroseSugar cane, beet root
LactoseMilk and dairy products
StarchPotato, cereals like wheat, rice, maize
GlycogenAnimal liver

Plants store starch, animals glycogen; cellulose makes cell walls. Uses: building, paper, cotton clothing, 5% glucose drips.

Key Points

  • Carbohydrates have general formula Cx(H2O)y and give instant energy.
  • They are polyhydroxy aldehydes or ketones, made by photosynthesis.
  • Classes differ by sugar units: mono 1, oligo 2-10, poly more than 10.
  • Starch, glycogen and cellulose are polysaccharides of glucose.

lessons.title: 13.2 Proteins
lessons.notes_html:
Proteins are giant bio-organic compounds formed by joining amino acids. From Greek proteios (first); vital to every cell.

Roles in the Body

  • As skin, hair, cartilage, muscles, tendons and ligaments, they hold together, protect and give structure.
  • As enzymes, hormones, antibodies and globulins, they catalyse, regulate and protect body chemistry.
  • As haemoglobin, myoglobin and lipoproteins, they transport oxygen and other substances.

13.2.1 Amino Acids as Building Blocks

An amino acid has both an amino group -NH2 and a carboxyl group -COOH in one molecule, on a central carbon with H and an R (alkyl) chain. Human proteins use 20 different amino acids: 10 are made by the body and the remaining 10 essential amino acids must be taken in food. When amino acids join, a water molecule is eliminated and the joining bond is a peptide bond. Thousands linked by peptide bonds form a protein, which folds to save space; on hydrolysis a protein gives back its amino acids.

13.2.2 Sources and Uses

Protein is the basic body stuff; the dry mass of animals is about 50% protein. Plants make their own protein, animals mostly take amino acids in food. Sources: meat, eggs, beans, lentils, pulses, dry fruits and seeds.

  • Main stuff of the body, present in almost every tissue.
  • Act as carriers of substances in the body.
  • Act as catalysts (enzymes) - without them body functions stop; also serve as hormones.
  • Leather, a protein, is used for shoes, clothes and sports articles.

Key Points

  • Proteins are polymers of amino acids joined by peptide bonds.
  • Each amino acid has -NH2 and -COOH groups and an R chain.
  • Of 20 amino acids, 10 are essential and must come from food.
  • Proteins build the body and work as enzymes, hormones and carriers.

lessons.title: 13.3 Lipids
lessons.notes_html:
Lipids are long-chained esters of fatty acids and glycerol (glycerine). Members include fats, steroids, terpenes and waxes. Fats are triesters of glycerol and long-chained carboxylic acids (alkyl chains R1, R2, R3), yield a lot of energy, and are taken as animal fat, margarine, butter and cream. Oils are unsaturated, liquid at normal temperature, usually in plant products.

Steroids and Waxes

Steroids have a characteristic four condensed rings structure. They act as hormones, e.g. male and female sex hormones testosterone and progesterone, and steroidal compounds in bile juices help digestion. Waxes coat leaves and stems and prevent plants losing excessive water, e.g. Corunda wax on Brazilian palm leaves, used in floor and automobile waxes; lanolin coats lambs wool. Waxes give lubrication, protection and energy storage, and are used in ointments, hand creams and cosmetics.

13.3.1 Fatty Acids

Fatty acids are the bio-organic compounds that form lipids: carboxylic acids with a -COOH group and a long chain of unbranched carbons as a tail, e.g. palmitic acid (C15H31COOH) and stearic acid (C17H35COOH).

13.3.2 Sources and Uses of Lipids

In animals lipids are found as fats and in milk; in plants as oils. They are a source of large energy, increase the taste of food (butter, ghee, oils), are used as stored fat by hibernating animals, and fatty tissues protect humans and animals from severe cold. Oily layers protect desert plants from transpiration. Many oils and fats are used as drugs, e.g. cod liver oil.

Key Points

  • Lipids are long-chained esters of fatty acids and glycerol.
  • Fats are solid diet lipids; oils are unsaturated and liquid at normal temperature.
  • Steroids have four condensed rings and act as hormones.
  • Lipids store large energy and insulate the body against cold.

lessons.title: 13.4 Nucleic Acids
lessons.notes_html:
Nucleic acids are the special biopolymers responsible for heredity. There are two types: DNA (Deoxyribose nucleic acid) and RNA (Ribose nucleic acid). They carry genetic information in the sequence of their subunits, called nucleotides. A nucleotide directs production of a specific protein, and these proteins run the cells, so the body acts under the command of DNA and RNA built genes. Small differences in DNA sequences cause the diversity of life; the genetic material of humans and chimpanzees differs by only 3%.

13.4.1 DNA

DNA gives us our identity and controls cell functioning; its instructions make each tissue behave separately. Its complicated structure was discovered by J-Watson and F-Crick in 1953. Each nucleotide is made of a phosphate group, a pentose sugar and a nitrogenous base. DNA has 4 bases: Adenine, Cytosine, Thiamine and Guanine (A, T, C, G). Their sequence forms the code of DNA; each gene has its distinct code. Two strands run parallel, so DNA is a double-stranded giant structure.

13.4.2 RNA

RNA is the second type, like DNA but single-stranded. Its nucleotide also has 3 basic groups, with two differences: its pentose sugar is ribose instead of deoxyribose, and the base uracil replaces thiamine. RNA carries messages from DNA, forms different proteins on the command of DNA, and these proteins catalyse and control cell reactions and processes. In a DNA test, the characteristic sequence inherited from parents is matched.

Key Points

  • Nucleic acids are of two types: DNA and RNA, the units of heredity.
  • A nucleotide consists of a phosphate group, a pentose sugar and a nitrogenous base.
  • DNA is double-stranded, with bases A, T, C and G; its structure was given by Watson and Crick in 1953.
  • RNA is single-stranded, has ribose sugar and uracil instead of thiamine.

lessons.title: 13.5 Vitamins
lessons.notes_html:
Vitamins are organic compounds needed in the diet for normal body health. The name was given by Polish biochemist Kazimierz Funk in 1912, from Latin vita (life) and amin (amine). They are essential for normal growth and health, act as catalysts or co-enzymes, and prevent and cure many diseases.

13.5.1 Types of Vitamins

  • Water-soluble: vitamin-B and vitamin-C. Excreted in urine, so taken daily. Vitamin-B is a group (B1, B2, etc.).
  • Fat-soluble (water-insoluble): vitamin-A, D, E and K. Stored in body tissues, so not needed daily.
VitaminSolubilityDaily requirementDeficiency diseaseSources
Vitamin-AFat900 ugNight-blindnessAnimal tissues, especially fish and liver
Vitamin-BWater1.2-1.5 mgBeriberi, anemiaMeats, leafy green vegetables, grains, legumes
Vitamin-CWater90.0 mgScurvyCitrus fruits, strawberries, tomatoes, leafy green vegetables
Vitamin-DFat5.0-10 ugRickets and OsteomalaciaSynthesized in skin in sunlight; fortified foods

13.5.2 Importance of Vitamins

Vitamins mostly play their role in metabolic pathways. Taken in increased amount, fat-soluble vitamins (e.g. vitamin-A) can cause disease - hypervitaminosis, whose common symptoms are nausea and vomiting.

Key Points

  • Vitamins are needed in small amounts for growth, health and metabolism.
  • Vitamin-B and C are water-soluble and are required daily.
  • Vitamins A, D, E and K are fat-soluble and are stored in the body.
  • Lack of A causes night-blindness, B causes beriberi, C causes scurvy and D causes rickets.

lessons.title: 14.1 Composition of the Atmosphere
lessons.notes_html:
What is the Atmosphere?

The atmosphere is the layer of gases that covers our planet earth. This mixture of gases is commonly known as air. Compared with the diameter of the earth, the atmosphere is very thin and lasts up to about 500 km. It has no definite boundary; it slowly thins and finally fades into outer space.

Composition of Air

GasPercentage
Nitrogen78%
Oxygen (O2)20.95%
Argon0.93%
Carbon dioxide (CO2)0.04%
Water vapoursabout 1%
Other gasestrace amounts

Importance of the Atmosphere

  • All living things rely on air for normal life processes, e.g. respiration.
  • It serves as a thermo blanket which maintains a specific temperature for organisms.
  • Its coating of gases protects the earth and life from the hazardous radiation of space.
  • The constituents are present in different layers, each having a distinct character. Any change in composition could be fatal to all life forms, so it must be maintained as it is.

Key Points

  • Atmosphere is the layer of gases covering the earth, extending to about 500 km with no definite boundary.
  • Air contains 78% nitrogen, 20.95% oxygen, 0.93% argon and 0.04% carbon dioxide.
  • About 1% water vapours are also an important part of the atmosphere.
  • It acts as a thermo blanket and protects life from hazardous space radiation.

lessons.title: 14.2 The Layers of Atmosphere
lessons.notes_html:
The Layers of the Atmosphere

The atmosphere is made up of several layers, composed of different constituents, and each layer serves in a different way.

LayerExtentMain Features
TroposphereSurface to 7-14 kmLowest layer; about 75% of atmospheric mass
StratosphereUp to about 50 kmContains the ozone layer
MesosphereAbout 50 km to 90 kmColdest region; 20 C to -80 C
ThermosphereClosest to spaceHuge solar energy, but atoms far apart

Troposphere and Stratosphere

  • The troposphere is the only layer that can support life. Large amounts of water vapour are present, clouds develop here and birds fly here.
  • The stratosphere begins at the tropopause. Its importance is the ozone layer (ozonosphere), where ozone (O3), an allotropic form of oxygen, absorbs UV radiation. The energy is radiated as IR, heating this layer.
  • Without ozone, UV radiations would flood the earth and destroy life.

Mesosphere and Thermosphere

  • In the mesosphere, temperature falls as we move upward. Oxygen, nitrogen and carbon dioxide amounts are almost the same as near the surface, water vapour is very low, and meteors burn up here, seen as shooting stars.
  • The thermosphere has huge energy from solar radiations, but atoms are few and far apart, so heat transfer is too low and overall heat remains low and harmless.

Key Points

  • Four layers: troposphere, stratosphere, mesosphere and thermosphere.
  • Troposphere (7-14 km) holds about 75% of the mass and is the only life-supporting layer.
  • Stratosphere extends to about 50 km and contains the protective ozone layer.
  • Mesosphere (50-90 km) is the coldest layer, from 20 C to -80 C; meteors burn up in it.
  • Thermosphere is closest to space; its overall heat remains low despite huge energy.

lessons.title: 14.3 Environmental Pollution and Pollutants
lessons.notes_html:
Pollution and Pollutants

A pollutant is a substance that contaminates the earth's environment, affecting quality of life or the natural functioning of ecosystems. Its coming into the environment is environmental pollution. Some is natural (volcanic eruptions); most is caused by human activities.

  • Biodegradable pollutants: decompose rapidly by natural processes, e.g. sewage, CO, CO2, SO2, NO, NO2. A problem when added faster than they decompose.
  • Non-degradable pollutants: do not decompose, or decompose slowly, e.g. CFCs, dioxin pesticides, plastics, radioactive materials; difficult or impossible to remove.

Types: air pollution, water pollution, soil contamination, noise pollution, visual pollution. This chapter deals with air pollution from industry and motor vehicles.

Major Air Pollutants

  • Primary pollutants pollute directly: SO2, NOx, COx, hydrocarbons, dust, ash, smoke.
  • Secondary pollutants pollute indirectly, produced by primary pollutants: ground level ozone, smog (smoke + fog, severe in winter).
  • SO2: burning coal/oil containing sulphur; causes acid rain. NO2: high temperature combustion; also acid rain.
  • CO: incomplete combustion of natural gas, coal or wood; vehicular exhaust is a major source.
  • CO2: emitted in combustion; causes the greenhouse effect (increase in temperature of the earth's atmosphere).
  • Particulates: smoke, dust, poisonous lead; 2.5-10 micrometers, enter nasal cavity, bronchia and lungs.
  • CFCs: contain Cl and F; from spray paints, Freon refrigerant, DDT; harmful to the ozone layer.
  • Others: radioactive pollutants (nuclear explosions, hospitals), ground level ozone (poisonous; high-voltage equipment), odours (garbage, sewage).

Key Points

  • A pollutant contaminates the environment; its entry is environmental pollution.
  • Biodegradable pollutants decompose rapidly; non-degradable ones like CFCs and plastics do not.
  • Primary pollutants act directly; secondary pollutants like smog act indirectly.
  • SO2 and NO2 cause acid rain; CO2 causes the greenhouse effect; CFCs harm ozone.

lessons.title: 14.4 The Acid Rain and Its Effects
lessons.notes_html:
What is Acid Rain?

Acid rain is rainfall that has a pH level of less than 5.6. It is caused chiefly by two types of oxides: sulphur oxides and nitrogen oxides. These oxides combine with moisture in the atmosphere to make sulphuric acid and nitric acid.

Formation of Acid Rain

  • Sulphur dioxide reacts with the oxygen of air to give SO3, which combines with water to form sulphuric acid:

2SO2(g) + O2(g) -> 2SO3(g)

SO3(g) + H2O(l) -> H2SO4(aq)

  • Oxides of nitrogen combine with water of the atmosphere to form acidic products:

2NO2(g) + H2O(l) -> HNO3(aq) + HNO2(aq)

These acids can be carried far from their origin in clouds and then come down as rainfall.

Effects of Acid Rain

  • It directly destroys the life forms where it falls.
  • It has adverse impacts on forests, freshwaters and soils.
  • It kills off insect and aquatic life forms.
  • It causes damage to buildings and has possible impacts on human health.

To prevent acid rains, international treaties (e.g. Montreal and Kyoto treaties) on the long-range transport of atmospheric pollutants have been agreed, which have significantly reduced the emission of hazardous gases and thus cut down acid rains.

Key Points

  • Acid rain is rainfall with pH less than 5.6.
  • It is formed when sulphur and nitrogen oxides combine with atmospheric moisture to form H2SO4 and HNO3.
  • It damages forests, freshwaters, soils, buildings, aquatic life and human health.
  • Montreal and Kyoto treaties have reduced hazardous gas emissions and acid rains.

lessons.title: 14.5 Ozone Depletion and Its Effects
lessons.notes_html:
The Protective Ozone Layer

A protective layer of ozone gas is present in the upper atmosphere (stratosphere), which protects the earth from highly energetic and dangerous ultraviolet radiations:

O3(g) + uv -> O(g) + O2(g)

The O2 produced again combines with the atomic oxygen to yield the ozone back:

O2(g) + O(g) -> O3(g)

How CFCs Deplete Ozone

In the late 1970s, scientists found that chemicals called chlorofluorocarbons (CFCs) damage this protective layer. Chlorine from CFCs reacts with ozone in a chain reaction:

Cl(g) + O3(g) -> ClO(g) + O2(g)

O3(g) -> O(g) + O2(g) (in UV light)

ClO(g) + O(g) -> Cl(g) + O2(g)

This is a chain reaction: a single chlorine atom depletes thousands of ozone molecules, so ozone is constantly depleting.

Effects of Ozone Depletion

  • More UV radiation reaches the earth's surface, which is expected to increase skin cancer in humans.
  • Increased UV radiations destroy micro-organisms, thus imbalancing the entire ecosystem.
  • The increase in UV also causes global warming directly and indirectly.
  • The ozone hole so far discovered is at the Antarctic region, where life is not so abundant, so damage to life has not yet been caused by this hole, but measures are required to stop this damage.
  • An important step taken is the ban on the usage of CFCs.

Note: ozone itself is poisonous at ground level, where sparks in electric equipment produce it; ground level ozone is a form of air pollution.

Key Points

  • Ozone in the stratosphere protects the earth from dangerous UV radiations.
  • Ozone is formed back by O2 + O -> O3, keeping a natural cycle.
  • CFCs release chlorine, and one chlorine atom destroys thousands of ozone molecules in a chain reaction.
  • Ozone depletion increases skin cancer, destroys micro-organisms and causes global warming.
  • The ozone hole is over the Antarctic region; banning CFCs is the key protective step.

lessons.title: 15.1 Water and Properties of Water
lessons.notes_html:
Water on Earth

Water is an essential part of all living forms. The water of the Earth is called the hydrosphere. It is used on a large scale for drinking, washing and cultivation, yet the water actually available to humans is limited, so water scarcity is common in most areas.

Water covers 71% of the Earth's surface.

PartShare
Salt water (oceans and ground saline water)97.5%
Fresh water2.5%
Fresh water in glaciers and polar ice caps68.7% of fresh water
Ground water30.1% of fresh water
Surface water1.2% of fresh water
Water available for our useabout 0.7% of total water

The Water Cycle

Water moves perpetually through the water cycle: evaporation, transpiration, precipitation and run-off, usually reaching the sea. Humans have disturbed this cycle for centuries, more so with industrialization.

Properties of Water (15.1.1)

Pure water, H2O, is colourless and tasteless.

  • At normal temperature and pressure it is a liquid.
  • It is a neutral compound; it shows no acidic or basic properties.
  • It dissolves many inorganic and organic substances.
  • Ice is less dense than liquid water, so ice floats on the sea and life underneath continues to grow.
  • It has a high heat capacity, 4.18 Jg-1 C-1. It absorbs heat in the day, so the Earth's temperature does not fall too low at night.

Key Points

  • Water covers 71% of the Earth's surface; 97.5% is salt water and only 2.5% is fresh water.
  • Only about 0.7% of the total water is available for human use.
  • The water cycle works by evaporation, transpiration, precipitation and run-off.
  • Pure water is colourless, tasteless and neutral, with formula H2O.
  • Ice is less dense than water, so it floats; water has a high heat capacity of 4.18 Jg-1 C-1.

lessons.title: 15.2 Water as a Solvent
lessons.notes_html:
An Excellent Solvent

Water as a solvent: water is an excellent solvent. It dissolves most inorganic and many organic compounds.

Structure of Water

  • Water is made of two kinds of atoms: oxygen and hydrogen.
  • The angle between the H-O-H atoms is 104.45 degrees.
  • The O-H distance is 0.9584 A.
  • Pure water boils at 100 C and freezes at 0 C.

Why Water Dissolves So Much

This high solubility is due to the polar nature of water. The shared electrons are attracted towards the central oxygen, so oxygen carries a partial negative charge and each hydrogen carries a partial positive charge.

When a substance dissolves, the negative part of the solute is captured by the positive part of water, and the positive part of the solute is attracted by the negative part of water. The solute particles are thus dissolved. This process is called solvation.

In the solvation of table salt, NaCl, the polar substance breaks up into ions. The ions are masked by water molecules through their poles, and new forces develop in this solute-solvent interaction.

Key Points

  • Water dissolves most inorganic and many organic compounds.
  • The H-O-H angle is 104.45 degrees and the O-H distance is 0.9584 A.
  • Pure water boils at 100 C and freezes at 0 C.
  • Water is polar: oxygen is partly negative and hydrogen is partly positive.
  • Solvation is the process in which water molecules surround the parts or ions of a solute and dissolve it, as with NaCl.

lessons.title: 15.3 Soft and Hard Water and Types of Hardness
lessons.notes_html:
Soft and Hard Water (15.3)

Hard water is water rich in mineral contents, especially calcium and magnesium ions and their bicarbonates and sulphates. Water without these minerals is soft water.

When rain water passes through places where these minerals occur, the ions enter the water by leaching from minerals in an aquifer. Common calcium minerals are calcite and gypsum; a common magnesium mineral is dolomite, which also contains calcium. The CO2 in this process can be absorbed from the atmosphere.

CaCO3(s) + CO2(g) + H2O(l) -> Ca2+(aq) + 2HCO3-(aq)

MgCO3(s) + CO2(g) + H2O(l) -> Mg2+(aq) + 2HCO3-(aq)

Soap test: hard water does not lather with soap, but soft water lathers easily.

Types of Hardness (15.4)

TypeCauseRemoval
Temporary hardnessCa2+ and HCO3- ions, e.g. Ca(HCO3)2Easily removed, e.g. by warming
Permanent hardnessSulphates of Ca2+ or Mg2+, or bothNot removed by simple methods or heating; needs e.g. ion exchange

On heating, calcium bicarbonate changes into insoluble carbonate, which settles down; decantation then gives water free of it:

Ca(HCO3)2(s) + heat -> CaCO3(s) + CO2(g) + H2O(g)

Permanent hardness salts become more soluble on heating, so they cannot be removed by heating.

Key Points

  • Hard water is rich in Ca2+ and Mg2+ ions and their bicarbonates and sulphates.
  • Minerals enter rain water by leaching from calcite, gypsum and dolomite.
  • Hard water does not lather with soap; soft water lathers easily.
  • Temporary hardness is due to bicarbonates and is removed by warming.
  • Permanent hardness is due to sulphates of Ca2+ or Mg2+ and is not removed by heating.

lessons.title: 15.5 Methods of Removing Hardness and Disadvantages of Hard Water
lessons.notes_html:
Removal of Temporary Hardness (15.5)

The method of water softening depends on the ions that made the water hard. Temporary hardness is relatively easy to remove.

  • By boiling: on boiling, the bicarbonate changes to insoluble carbonate. The solid precipitate is removed by decantation or filtration. Ca(HCO3)2(s) -> CaCO3(s) + H2O(l) + CO2(g)
  • Clark's method: slaked lime is added; it converts dissolved bicarbonates into insoluble carbonates. Ca(HCO3)2(aq) + Ca(OH)2(aq) -> 2CaCO3(s) + 2H2O(l)

Removal of Permanent Hardness

Permanent hard water contains sulphates or chlorides of calcium or magnesium. It is removed by ion exchangers such as sodium or potassium zeolites, or by soluble sodium/potassium carbonates (washing soda), which also act as ion exchangers.

Na2CO3(aq) + CaSO4(aq) -> CaCO3(s) + Na2SO4(aq)

Na2-zeolite + CaSO4(aq) -> Ca-zeolite + Na2SO4(aq)

Disadvantages of Hard Water (15.6)

  • Soap or shampoo does not lather, so skin, scalp and clothes are not cleaned well.
  • Insoluble salts left by shampoo make hair rougher and harder to detangle.
  • Salts deposit inside boilers and pipes. The deposits can block the passage of steam, the system can blow up, and such accidents have caused loss of lives many times.

Key Points

  • Temporary hardness is removed by boiling or by Clark's method using slaked lime.
  • Boiling converts Ca(HCO3)2 into insoluble CaCO3, removed by decantation or filtration.
  • Permanent hardness is removed by ion exchange with zeolites or washing soda.
  • Hard water wastes soap and cleans skin, hair and clothes poorly.
  • Scale in boilers and pipes can block steam and cause dangerous explosions.

lessons.title: 15.7 Water Pollution and Water Borne Diseases
lessons.notes_html:
Water Pollution (15.7)

Water pollution is the adverse effect on lakes, rivers, oceans and ground water by contamination made by humans. A major cause is industrial waste with heavy metals like lead, arsenic and mercury, plus organic toxins, insecticides and oils. It is a direct result of industrialization.

Waste typeMain pollutants
Industrial wastes (15.7.1)Sewage of industries or mines; heavy metals and toxins that endanger aquatic life and harm humans using the water
Household wastes (15.7.2)Organic debris with germs of hepatitis, cholera, GIT diseases and typhoid; insecticides, pesticides, food wastes and polyethylene products
Agriculture wastes (15.7.3)Pesticides washed into reservoirs, killing life there; fertilizers that contaminate drinking water

Water Borne Diseases (15.8)

Water borne diseases are caused by drinking or handling contaminated water. Pesticides and mercury compounds can cause death; high fluoride can cause abnormalities in bone formation. Contamination enters the food chain through fish eaten by birds, animals and humans.

  • Gastro: gastro-intestinal diseases, including cholera and diarrhoea; most common in our country, kills thousands each year.
  • Hepatitis: damages the liver; caused by a virus in contaminated water.
  • GIT worms: round, hook, tape, pin and whip worms; cause diarrhoea, anaemia, itching and irritation.
  • Jaundice: yellow discoloration of skin and whites of the eyes due to increased bilirubin in blood; often seen in hepatitis.
  • Typhoid fever: bacterial, spread by contaminated water; fatal if not treated well. Malaria is linked indirectly.

Making Water Drinkable

A 3-stage filter: (1) sediment filter sieves out particles; (2) activated carbon filter absorbs odorous and coloured substances; (3) UV disinfection kills germs. Replace the charcoal unit when its pores fill up.

Key Points

  • Water pollution is human contamination of lakes, rivers, oceans and ground water.
  • Its main types are industrial, household and agriculture wastes.
  • Water borne diseases include gastro, cholera, hepatitis, typhoid and jaundice.
  • A 3-stage filter uses sediment filtration, activated carbon and UV disinfection.

lessons.title: 16.1 Basic Metallurgical Operations
lessons.notes_html:
Industrial Chemistry and Metallurgy

Industrial chemistry deals with preparing chemical compounds in bulk in factories, e.g. aspirin, so that laboratory knowledge is used in daily life.

Metallurgy is the study of the structure and properties of metals, with special reference to their extraction from the ground, and the procedures for refining, alloying and making things from metals.

An ore is the raw mineral found in the earth crust from which a specific metal is extracted. There is no common process for all metals, because metals differ in chemical and physical properties and in their impurities, so each metal needs its own technique. Some operations are common to all metals.

The Four Metallurgical Operations

  • 1. Crushing and grinding of ore (pulverisation): ores occur in hard lumps; the first step is crushing and grinding the ore into small pieces in a proper mill, so it becomes ready for chemical procedures.
  • 2. Concentration of ore: the ground ore is concentrated by removing the major impurities present in it. This step is different for different metals.
  • 3. Extraction of metal from oxide ore: the ores, usually in the form of metal oxides, are treated chemically by a specific technique for each metal.
  • 4. Refining of crude metal: purifying the crude metal. Methods depend on the metal: distillation, electrolytic refining, zone refining, vapour-phase refining and chromatography.

Key Points

  • Metallurgy deals with extraction of pure metals from their ores.
  • An ore is the raw mineral from which a metal is extracted.
  • First step in metallurgy is crushing of the ore.
  • The four operations are crushing and grinding, concentration, extraction and refining.
  • Each metal needs its own technique because metals and their impurities differ.

lessons.title: 16.1.1 Metallurgy of Copper
lessons.notes_html:
Copper and Its Ores

Copper is used in almost every electrical instrument for its excellent electrical conduction and high resistance to corrosion, and also in utensils and alloys, e.g. brass and bronze. The earth crust contains only 0.007% copper, not uniformly distributed.

Ores include chalcopyrite (CuFeS2), bornite (Cu5FeS4), covellite (CuS), chalcocite (Cu2S), azurite (Cu3(CO3)2(OH)2), malachite (Cu2CO3(OH)2) and cuprite (Cu2O). The sulphide ores are more abundant.

Concentration by Froth Flotation

The crushed ore powder is mixed with chemicals in a water bath (aeration tank) containing surfactant. Air is forced through the slurry; hydrophobic copper sulphide particles catch onto the bubbles, rise as froth and are skimmed off; the remainder is discarded as tailings. The concentrate (CuS) contains about 40% Cu.

Extraction

FeS is removed with SiO2 and lime at 1200 C: 2FeS + 3O2 + 2SiO2 -> 2FeO.SiO2 + 2SO2. The FeO.SiO2 slag is discarded; the remaining material, almost 70% Cu, is copper matte. Air blown through the matte gives: 2Cu2S + 3O2 -> 2Cu2O + 2SO2 and Cu2S + 2Cu2O -> 6Cu + SO2. Copper up to 98% purity is called blister copper.

Electrolytic Refining

Blister copper is refined in a cell with 3-4% copper sulphate and 10-16% sulphuric acid; the cathode is pure copper and only 0.2-0.4 volts is needed. Anode: Cu -> Cu2+ + 2e-. Cathode: Cu2+ + 2e- -> Cu. Silver, gold, selenium and tellurium settle as anode mud, a valuable byproduct; arsenic and zinc remain in solution. The refined copper is 99.9% pure.

Key Points

  • Earth crust contains 0.007% copper; chalcopyrite CuFeS2 is an important ore.
  • Froth flotation concentrates the sulphide ore to about 40% Cu.
  • Copper matte contains almost 70% Cu; blister copper is 98% pure.
  • Electrolytic refining gives 99.9% pure copper.
  • Silver, gold, selenium and tellurium are recovered from anode mud.

lessons.title: 16.2 The Solvay Process
lessons.notes_html:
Soda Ash

The Solvay process prepares sodium carbonate, Na2CO3, commonly known as soda ash, an important chemical used widely in industries and at homes. In 2005 world production of soda ash was about 42 billion kilograms; almost three-fourths came through the Solvay process and the remainder was mined directly.

The process was developed by Ernest Solvay during the 1860s. It is successful because it is very simple, uses cheap raw materials, NaCl and CaCO3, and gives soda ash of good purity. Overall: 2NaCl + CaCO3 -> Na2CO3 + CaCl2.

Steps of the Process

  • Ammoniation: saturated NaCl solution (brine) flows down an ammoniating tower, where NH3 gas is mixed with it.
  • Carbonation: ammoniated brine trickles down the carbonating (Solvay) tower and meets CO2 from heating limestone in a kiln: CaCO3 -> CaO + CO2.
  • 2NH3 + CO2 + H2O -> (NH4)2CO3; then (NH4)2CO3 + CO2 + H2O -> 2NH4HCO3.
  • NH4HCO3 + NaCl -> NaHCO3 + NH4Cl. The lower part of the tower is cooled, NaHCO3 precipitates, and it is separated by vacuum filtration and washed.
  • Calcination: NaHCO3 is dried and heated in a rotary furnace called a calciner: 2NaHCO3 -> Na2CO3 + CO2 + H2O. The CO2 is recirculated.

Recovery of Ammonia

CaO from the kiln is treated with water: CaO + H2O -> Ca(OH)2. Then 2NH4Cl + Ca(OH)2 -> CaCl2 + 2NH3 + 2H2O, so the NH3 is recovered and reused. In the flow sheet, A = Ammoniation Tower, B = Solvay Tower, C = Kiln, D = Ammonia Recovery Tower.

Key Points

  • Solvay process prepares soda ash, Na2CO3, from NaCl and CaCO3.
  • It was developed by Ernest Solvay in the 1860s.
  • NaHCO3 is precipitated in the Solvay tower and heated in a calciner to give Na2CO3.
  • CO2 is recirculated and NH3 is recovered from NH4Cl with Ca(OH)2.
  • Almost three-fourths of world soda ash is made by this process.

lessons.title: 16.3 Urea
lessons.notes_html:
What is Urea?

Urea, or carbamide, is a well known fertilizer used throughout the world and in Pakistan. Its molecular formula is CO(NH2)2, also written NH2CONH2. It was the first organic compound synthesized, in 1828 by Wohler.

Urea is important as a nitrogen source for plants. Being slightly basic, it also reduces the acidity of the soil produced by the decaying action of organic matter. Fertilizers are needed because crops remove nutrients from the soil; urea is preferred in Pakistan over ammonia fertilizer because it is a solid that is easy to store, transport and spread.

Commercial Preparation

On a commercial scale urea is prepared from CO2 and NH3: 2NH3 + CO2 -> CO(NH2)2 + H2O. The industry works in steps:

  • Step 1: CO2 and H2 are prepared by the action of steam on natural gas over Ni catalyst: CH4 + 2H2O -> CO2 + 4H2.
  • Step 2: H2 is treated with N2 at 500 C over Fe2O3 to obtain NH3: N2 + 3H2 -> 2NH3.
  • Step 3: CO2 and NH3 combine to give ammonium carbamate: 2NH3 + CO2 -> NH2COONH4.
  • Step 4: Ammonium carbamate is dehydrated by heating: NH2COONH4 -> CO(NH2)2 + H2O. Ammonium carbamate is thus the hydrated form of urea.
  • Step 5: Water is evaporated; the molten urea is sprayed in a cooled tower, where the drops solidify as small prills, which are filled in bags and sent to market.

Key Points

  • Urea (carbamide), CO(NH2)2, is a nitrogen fertilizer first synthesized by Wohler in 1828.
  • Commercially it is prepared from ammonia and carbon dioxide.
  • Natural gas and steam are the starting raw materials.
  • Ammonium carbamate forms first, then loses water to give urea.
  • Molten urea is sprayed in a cooled tower to form prills.

lessons.title: 16.4 Petroleum Industry
lessons.notes_html:
Petroleum

Petroleum comes from Greek words: Petra meaning rock and Oleum meaning oil. It is a blackish or brownish black, viscous liquid drilled out from under the earth, a complex mixture of thousands of organic compounds separated into fractions at refineries. It fulfils almost all energy requirements, and industries such as plastics depend on it.

16.4.1 Origin of Petroleum

Petroleum originated by the action of bacteria, heat and pressure upon dead organic matter buried over time. Sea animals and plants died, fell to the sea bottom and were covered by mud; as temperature and pressure increased the remains were slowly cooked into crude oil. Such fuels are called fossil fuels.

16.4.2 Mining of Petroleum

Petroleum is trapped in channels and taken out through tubes from oil wells; it is found at more depth than water. Primary recovery (underground pressure) recovers about 20% of the oil, secondary recovery another 5 to 10%, and tertiary recovery reduces the viscosity of the oil to bring more to the surface.

16.4.3 Important Fractions of Petroleum

Refining uses fractional distillation, separating fractions by their different boiling points. As carbon atoms per molecule increase, boiling point and density both increase; fractions with more than 40 carbon atoms may be solid or semi-solid.

FractionCarbon atomsBoiling rangeUse

Octane Number

Fuel quality is measured by the octane number: higher the number, higher the performance. The standard is 100; petrol pumps in Pakistan sell gasoline of 80 octane number. It is increased by adding TEL (tetra ethyl lead), which causes environmental problems, or BTX (benzene, toluene, xylene), a relatively lesser pollutant.

Key Points

  • Petra is a Greek word meaning rock; petroleum means rock oil.
  • Petroleum formed by bacteria, heat and pressure on buried organic matter.
  • Primary recovery gives about 20% of the oil; secondary gives 5-10% more.
  • More carbon atoms in a fraction mean higher boiling point and density.
  • Octane number measures fuel efficiency; standard 100, in Pakistan petrol is 80.
  • LPG is propane and butane; the major fraction in CNG is methane.
